title: Deviation from goal pace, body temperature and body mass loss as predictors of road race performance
authors: Adams WM, Hosokawa Y, Belval LN, Huggins RA, Stearns RL, Casa DJ
journal: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
population: Active runners with a gastrointestinal temperature pill and a GPS heart-rate watch in the 2014 Falmouth Road Race (11.3 km, warm weather)
findings: Percent off predicted pace was calculated for seven segments of the race.
Percent off predicted pace during the first mile significantly predicted overall finish time (R2 = 0.64).
Larger percent body mass loss was associated with faster finish times (R2 = 0.19, p = 0.018) and faster average pace (R2 = 0.29, p = 0.012).
Gastrointestinal temperature at the finish was not predictive of finish time (p > 0.05); there was a trend to a slower pace in runners finishing at 40 C or above.

Overall, finish time was influenced by greater variations in pace during the first two miles; runners who minimised fluid losses and had lower gastrointestinal temperature were associated with meeting self-predicted goals.
limitations: The sample size and the confidence intervals are not in the abstract (the record's sampleSize is null for that reason); one 11.3 km race in the warm; the body-mass-loss and goal-pace results are associations in a self-selected sample.
implications: The only 10 km-class road race record in the corpus with pace by segment: in a warm 11.3 km race the first two miles' deviation from predicted pace, not later pace, tracked the finish time. Weak support for a 10 km pacing sentence about the opening; says nothing on fluid targets (body mass loss went with faster finishes).

verification.notes: Crossref matches (JSAMS 20:302-306). Abstract read on Europe PMC; the percent-sign text after 'R2 = 0.64' is garbled in the indexed abstract and the p value there is omitted. Crossref lists no correction, erratum or retraction notice (checked 2026-11-16).
